claims.text: The dynamic mechanical response of solidified Co-free FeNiCrMn is primarily governed by dislocation dynamics.
Chemical short-range-order fluctuations act as variable obstacles to dislocation motion in FeNiCrMn.
Increasing strain rate enhances dislocation pile-up and thereby increases strength.
Increasing temperature promotes thermally activated dislocation bypass and dynamic recovery, thereby reducing strength.
The proposed initial FeNiCrMn microstructure is chemically disordered and single-phase, with no secondary precipitates.
Temperature and strain rate will be varied under controlled tensile or compressive loading.
The proposed simulation temperature range is approximately 200 K to 700 K.
At lower temperatures or higher strain rates, dislocations have insufficient thermal energy or time to overcome local compositional obstacles, resulting in higher yield stress.
At higher temperatures or lower strain rates, enhanced dislocation motion and dynamic recovery reduce yield stress.
Yield stress should increase monotonically with increasing strain rate over the proposed regime.
Yield stress should decrease with increasing temperature over the proposed regime.
Dislocation pile-up and dynamic-recovery rates will correlate with the predicted yield-stress changes.
At room temperature and a moderate strain rate, dislocation pinning and thermal activation are expected to be balanced.
The hypothesis is restricted to homogenized, single-phase Co-free FeNiCrMn under conditions without phase transformations or secondary precipitation.
Long-term annealing or extreme deformation conditions may produce microstructural evolution beyond dislocation dynamics and invalidate the hypothesis.
Molecular-dynamics simulations may inadequately capture long-range diffusion and precipitation kinetics when extrapolated to experimental timescales.
A lack of the predicted strain-rate and temperature trends, or a lack of correlation between local chemical order and dislocation pinning, would falsify the hypothesis.
